# Angiotensin Receptor–Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Rationale and pharmacology

Heart failure (HF) management has long centred on antagonising the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) and sympathetic activation, but the natriuretic peptide system—which promotes natriuresis, vasodilation, and suppression of maladaptive remodelling—represents a complementary target. Because neprilysin degrades natriuretic peptides as well as angiotensin II and bradykinin, its inhibition augments these protective hormones [1]. Early efforts to combine neprilysin inhibition with ACE inhibition foundered: in the OVERTURE trial, the vasopeptidase inhibitor omapatrilat was not superior to enalapril and carried an excess of angioedema, attributed to simultaneous inhibition of ACE, neprilysin, and aminopeptidase P [2]. The OVERTURE trial randomly assigned 5770 patients with NYHA class II to IV heart failure to double-blind treatment with either enalapril or the ACE-NEP inhibitor omapatrilat for a mean of 14.5 months.

These lessons informed the design of LCZ696 (sacubitril/valsartan), a supramolecular complex pairing the neprilysin-inhibitor prodrug sacubitril with the angiotensin-receptor blocker valsartan, thereby avoiding ACE inhibition and reducing angioedema risk. LCZ696 treatment was associated with increases in plasma cGMP, renin concentration and activity, and angiotensin II, providing evidence for neprilysin inhibition and angiotensin receptor blockade. Twice-daily dosing maintains sustained dual inhibition [3]. A proof-of-concept phase 2 trial, PARAMOUNT, then evaluated the compound in HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). In patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, LCZ696 reduced NT-proBNP to a greater extent than did valsartan at 12 weeks and was well tolerated. [4]

## The PARADIGM-HF trial

The pivotal evidence came from PARADIGM-HF. In the PARADIGM-HF trial, the angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor sacubitril/valsartan was more effective than the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor enalapril in patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction. Overall, the sacubitril/valsartan versus enalapril hazard ratio for the primary composite end point was 0.80 (95% confidence interval, 0.73–0.87; P<0.001) and for cardiovascular death was 0.80 (0.71–0.89; P<0.001). [5] The benefit was consistent across background therapies including diuretics, digoxin, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and devices [6]. A pre-specified analysis additionally showed that in comparison with the enalapril group, fewer LCZ696-treated patients required intensification of medical treatment for heart failure or an emergency department visit for worsening heart failure. [7] Treatment effects were maintained even among patients requiring lower than target doses [8].

## Mechanisms: biomarkers and reverse remodelling

The mechanisms underlying clinical benefit have been clarified by dedicated studies. In the open-label PROVE-HF study, the reduction in NT-proBNP concentration achieved with sacubitril-valsartan was correlated—significantly but weakly—with signs of reverse cardiac remodeling at one year, including progressive improvements in LV ejection fraction and volumes [9]. By contrast, the randomised EVALUATE-HF trial found that among patients with HFrEF, sacubitril/valsartan versus enalapril did not reduce central aortic stiffness, while some measures of diastolic function improved. [10] Falling NT-proBNP itself carries prognostic weight in treated patients [11], supporting a model in which favourable neurohormonal modulation drives myocardial reverse remodelling.

## Initiation in and after hospitalisation

Because PARADIGM-HF excluded acutely decompensated patients, the PIONEER-HF trial tested in-hospital initiation. PIONEER-HF randomized 881 adults with acute decompensated HF and reduced EF to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril; sacubitril/valsartan was associated with a greater reduction in NT-proBNP than enalapril (−47% vs −25%), with similar rates of adverse reactions in either group. [12] Adjudicated clinical outcomes favoured early initiation: in patients hemodynamically stabilized during hospitalization, sacubitril/valsartan was associated with a significant reduction in the composite of death, rehospitalization for HF, LVAD implantation, or listing for transplantation (hazard ratio 0.54; 95% CI 0.37–0.79). [13] The open-label TRANSITION study confirmed feasibility, demonstrating that target dosing was attained in nearly half of patients whether initiation occurred pre- or post-discharge [14].

## Across the ejection-fraction spectrum

In HFpEF, the larger PARAGON-HF trial enrolled patients with LVEF ≥45%. The primary endpoint of total HF hospitalisations or cardiovascular death was narrowly missed (HR 0.87, CI 0.75–1.01; P=0.059). [15] Pre-specified subgroup analyses suggested benefit at the lower end of the EF range and among women [16]. A pooled analysis combining PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF indicated that the therapeutic effects of sacubitril/valsartan, compared with a RAS inhibitor alone, vary by LVEF, with treatment benefits, particularly for heart failure hospitalization, that appear to extend to patients with mildly reduced ejection fraction. [17] This concept was reinforced by the pooled PARAGLIDE-HF/PARAGON-HF analysis, in which sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced total worsening HF events and cardiovascular death among recently decompensated patients with higher EF [18].

## Guideline status

Contemporary guidelines reflect this evidence. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend ARNI as a foundational therapy for HFrEF [19], and the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline gives sacubitril/valsartan a Class 1 recommendation for HFrEF, designating ARNI a high-value therapy [20]. The 2023 ESC focused update integrated subsequent SGLT2-inhibitor data into the broader pillar-based framework [21].

## Conclusions

Sacubitril/valsartan transformed HFrEF therapy by reducing mortality and hospitalisation beyond RAAS inhibition alone, with mechanistic data pointing to reverse remodelling and biomarker reduction, and with feasible in-hospital initiation. Its role across higher ejection fractions remains nuanced, strongest in the mildly-reduced range and in women. Ongoing questions concern optimal sequencing with SGLT2 inhibitors, dosing in real-world populations, and cost-effectiveness, but ARNI is now firmly embedded as a cornerstone of guideline-directed medical therapy [22-30].
